_doc: cases (fm_*), plus ordinary/control sentences, multi-sentence inputs, and
varied difficulty-profile combinations (ctl_*). Each case carries its own
profile rather than sharing one global profile (tests/eval_corpus.txt's
convention), because §17's cases specifically need per-case profiles to
be meaningful. Phonetic claims in each case's 'notes' (onsets, shared
sounds) were verified against phonetic.py's live CMU-backed output before
being written here, not assumed from spelling.
'profile' fields map directly onto DifficultyProfile: sounds/words/
phrases are grapheme strings exactly as a user would type them;
'patterns' maps a word already in 'words' to a word-specific

cases.text: I thoroughly reviewed three reports and carefully examined the results.
cases.notes: Two unrelated flagged words (different onsets: reviewed=R, examined=no onset/vowel-initial) in one sentence. §17: 'no interaction modeling' is named as a persisting limitation, not solved by D′ - this case checks whether the two substitutions are still handled independently.

researcher/reported/results all have onset R (verified via phonetic.onset). The failure mode named in §17 is 'heavily-altered, obviously edited' output from touching every R-onset word independently. D′'s count-threshold escalation trigger (default >2 flagged content words) should fire here (3 flagged words) and restructure the whole sentence instead.

cases.text: I did not strongly agree with the stressful strategy.
cases.notes: strongly/stressful/strategy all onset S-T-R (verified). Forces restructuring escalation (3 flagged words). §17's concern: 'SBERT alone would likely accept a candidate that drops or flips not'. This is the direct test of semantic.negation_consistent() on a real generated restructuring, not a mocked candidate.

cases.text: I will present the object to the committee.
cases.notes: 'present' is a heteronym: verb (pri-ZENT, give/show) vs noun (PREZ-ent, gift) - flagged in difficulty_profile_test.py too. Verb sense here. Tests whether POS-gated WordNet lookup keeps candidates in the verb sense (e.g. 'introduce', 'submit') rather than contaminating with noun-sense synonyms ('gift').

cases.text: The gift was a wonderful present.
cases.notes: Same flagged word as fm_ambiguous_word_verb_sense, noun sense here. Direct comparison pair: does the same declared-difficult word get a sense-appropriate candidate in both sentences, or does one sense leak into the other?

cases.text: He runs the company every morning before he runs three miles.
cases.notes: 'runs' appears twice in one sentence with two different senses (manages vs. jogs), same POS tag (VBZ) both times - POS tagging alone cannot disambiguate. Tests whether both occurrences get the same (POS-tag-driven, sense-blind) candidate treatment or something more context-sensitive.

cases.text: Sarah Johnson uses TensorFlow for machine learning research.
cases.notes: 'Johnson' explicitly flagged as a word, and sound 't' matches TensorFlow's onset - both are proper nouns (NNP), which _SUBSTITUTABLE excludes regardless of profile match. This checks the protection actually holds under direct profile pressure, not just default indifference.

cases.text: Maria studies computer science at the local university. She particularly enjoys algorithms and data structures. Her research increasingly focuses on natural language processing.
cases.notes: Three sentences; 'structures' (2nd sentence) is the only str-onset word - cross-sentence pronoun reference ('She', 'Her' referring to Maria) is not modeled by any of the three systems under test, named as an explicit, unaddressed limitation in §17/§22. This checks each sentence is still processed independently and correctly, not that cross-sentence context is handled (it structurally isn't).

cases.text: The struggling student felt strongly stressed about the stressful strategy.
cases.notes: struggling/strongly/stressed/stressful/strategy all onset S-T-R (5 flagged words; 'student' onsets S-T only, verified NOT to match 'str'). §17: 'cannot restructure at all today - reports no valid synonym, leaves the word untouched' for the old pipelines; this is D′'s escalation path's clearest positive test case.

cases.source: n/a - ordinary sentence, no profile match
cases.text: The weather was pleasant during our walk yesterday afternoon.
cases.notes: No sound/word in this sentence matches an empty profile. Expected: no_change_needed status, byte-identical output, across all three systems.

cases.text: The team reached a strong decision after the meeting.
cases.notes: Exactly one str-onset word ('strong'). Simplest possible positive case - a clean, well-below-threshold single substitution, the case every system should handle well.
Very short input, one flagged onset ('absolutely' onset AH not B - actually no match expected; kept as a robustness/no-crash edge case rather than a guaranteed-positive one).

cases.text: The manager carefully reviewed the printed report before the morning meeting.
cases.notes: Three onsets chosen to hit most content words in the sentence (manager=M, carefully=K not flagged, reviewed=R, printed=P, report=R, before=B not flagged, morning=M, meeting=M) - deliberately close to or over D′'s degenerate-fraction pre-trigger (>0.6 of content words flagged). Tests the 'could not safely reformulate' path and whether it's reached gracefully rather than crashing or silently ignoring the density.

cases.text: I have a particular preference for the third option.
cases.notes: 'particular' flagged with problem_phones=['P'] (the word-initial P specifically), NOT promoted to a global sound. Neither grammar.py::SentenceRewriter nor rewrite/rewriter.py::DifficultyAwareRewriter has any concept of a word-specific sub-pattern - this case structurally cannot be represented in their profile inputs (only the word itself can be passed as blocked/always_replace), so it directly tests a capability gap between architectures, not just a quality difference.

cases.text: The weather was pleasant today. The strong wind made the strenuous hike difficult. We returned home before sunset.
cases.notes: Three sentences, only the middle one contains str-onset words (strong, strenuous). Tests that unflagged sentences pass through unchanged while the flagged one is handled, within one multi-sentence input.

cases.source: ROADMAP.md R13 - phrases declared but not consumed by any of the three systems
cases.text: We need to think outside the box for this particular challenge.
cases.notes: Only a phrase is declared, no sound/word. Expected (and this is the point of the case): no_change_needed / fully unaffected output from ALL THREE systems, since none of them currently consume difficulty_profile.phrases operationally - a known, already-documented gap, checked empirically here rather than just asserted in docs.

cases.text: She felt happy about the news from her sister.
cases.notes: 'happy' flagged. D′ has a WordNet antonym guard specifically to prevent 'happy'->'sad'/'unhappy'. Neither legacy pipeline has this guard - this checks whether the risk is real (do the legacy pipelines actually propose an antonym here) or purely theoretical.

cases.text: i dont think we shoud of presented the report that way, it wasnt very strong.
cases.notes: Informal, lower-case, contraction/spelling-error-laden input ('dont', 'shoud of', missing capitalization). grammar.py::sanitize_input() runs before all three systems in this evaluation (matching app.py's actual pipeline) - tests that grammar correction and reformulation compose sensibly, and that the flagged word ('strong') survives correction and still gets substituted.
